title: Two-Step and Multi-Step Binomial Trees: American Options, Early Exercise, Volatility Matching, and Continuous Dividends
prerequisites: One-step binomial pricing model, Delta hedging, and risk-neutral probability p
Option terminal payoffs and present value discounting
Basic concepts of volatility and continuous compounding
learningOutcomes: Construct a two-step binomial stock tree and backward-induction option valuation pricing framework ([fact-01], [fact-02]).
Calculate dynamic node Deltas and evaluate early exercise optimal boundaries for American options versus European options ([fact-03], [fact-05], [fact-06]).
Differentiate terminal gross cash payoffs from net trading profit (Profit = Payoff - Premium paid) ([fact-07]).
Apply Cox-Ross-Rubinstein volatility matching formulas and adjust risk-neutral probabilities for continuous dividend yields q ([fact-08], [fact-10]).
Understand multi-step convergence to Black-Scholes-Merton and recognize discrete jump risks during market crashes ([fact-09], [fact-11]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Early exercise is only optimal when the immediate intrinsic value exceeds the continuation value discounted from future nodes (max(Intrinsic, Continuation)). As shown at node B in Hull's example, holding an in-the-money option can retain higher time and continuation value than exercising prematurely ([fact-05], [fact-06]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Gross cash payoff (e.g., K - S) does not account for the initial premium paid to purchase the option. Net trading profit is strictly defined as Payoff minus Premium paid ([fact-07]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Because stock prices evolve and branch across nodes, Delta changes dynamically at every intermediate node and must be recalculated as Delta = (fu - fd) / (S_up - S_down) ([fact-03]).

activeRecallQuiz.scenario: Consider Hull's two-step American put option example with S0 = $50, K = $52, r = 5% per annum, T = 2 years, dt = 1 year, u = 1.2, d = 0.8, and risk-neutral probability p = 0.6282. At maturity (step 2), node C (down-down) has stock price $32 and put payoff $20, while step 1 node C has stock price $40 with continuation value $9.463 and initial option premium P0 = $5.09.
activeRecallQuiz.question: 1) Why is early exercise optimal at step 1 node C (S = $40)? 2) What is the net trading profit if the American put is exercised early at node C?
activeRecallQuiz.correctAnswer: Correctly identifying the downside risk and margin constraints.

coreTakeaways: Two-step binomial trees evaluate options by recursively discounting risk-neutral expected payoffs across intermediate and terminal nodes using backward induction ([fact-01], [fact-02]).

American options require evaluating max(Immediate Exercise Value, Continuation Value) at every node, generating an early exercise premium (e.g., $5.09 vs $4.19 for American vs European puts) ([fact-05], [fact-06]).

Cox-Ross-Rubinstein parameterization matches volatility sigma and adjusts for continuous dividend yields q, converging smoothly to Black-Scholes-Merton while remaining vulnerable to discrete jump risks ([fact-08], [fact-09], [fact-10], [fact-11]).
